item.content:encoded:
Although a familiar name to scholars of Yankees history (for lack of a better term), Tom Tresh did not have a long big-league career due to injuries and treatment of the time. Nonetheless, he was among the Bombers’ finest players of the 1960s and one of the last gasps of greatness from their vaunted farm system. As the team around him declined, Tresh continued to perform at a high level at multiple positions, making him a fan favorite and a valued final connection to those terrific teams of old.
Thomas Michael Tresh
Born: September 20, 1938 (Detroit, MI)
Died: October 14, 2008 (Venice, FL)
Yankees Tenure: 1961-69
September 1938 was a big month for the Tresh family, as patriarch Mike made his MLB debut with the Chicago White Sox on September 4th, and son Tom was born on September 20th. Mike Tresh spent 11 years catching for the South Siders, playing in over 1,000 games in the majors until ending his career in 1949 with Cleveland. He was named an All-Star by the Associated Press in 1945, the only year of the 20th century in which the Midsummer Classic wasn’t held (after the creation of the All-Star Game in 1933).
Tom Tresh spent some time living with his parents in an apartment in Chicago, but he went to school in Michigan, as his father’s career was over by then. At Allen Park High School in Detroit, he lettered in baseball, football, and basketball, and he later went to Central Michigan University in Mount Pleasant. His father’s prestigious job allowed him to gain some first-hand perspective on how clubhouses operated and what big-league living was like. He was even allowed to become a bat boy when his father briefly managed at Daytona Beach and Wausau, Wisconsin in 1951 and 1952, respectively.
MLB teams knew just how talented the younger Tresh was, and they kept a close scouting eye on him growing up. Mike and Doris Tresh wanted their son to go to college, but after a year at shortstop in Central Michigan, Tresh felt that he could not turn down a $30,000 offer from the New York Yankees. It was a lot of money for the time, the Yankees were baseball’s marquee team, and like many boys in the ’50s, Mickey Mantle was his idol. He recalled going to Tiger Stadium when the Yankees came to town and watching him intently from the upper deck in center field. Mike had even taught Tom how to switch-hit like Mantle.
Ultimately, Tresh was able to convince his parents to let him sign with the Yankees at age 19, assuring them that he would go back and finish his degree. He was on his way to joining his hero at Yankee Stadium.
Tresh was quick to impress in his first exposure to pro ball in 1958, as he hit .316/.435/.445 for the St. Petersburg Saints in 126 games of Class D ball. His pace slowed down upon a late-season promotion to the Double-A New Orleans Pelicans (no, not them), where the average player was seven years his senior.
It was around this time that Tresh met his idol for the first time, down in spring training. It was recalled in Jane Leavy’s book on Mantle, The Last Boy:
The first time he saw Mantle up close, Tresh was in an elevator during rookie camp in St. Pete--the doors opened and there he was. Though they stood eye to eye, Mantle seemed a thousand steps higher--a feeling Tresh never got over. “I never could see him as just one step higher than I was.”
After batting .246/.363/.415 in 133 games with the Binghamton Triplets in A-ball in 1960, the Yankees tested him at the minors’ highest level. There was no pressure to promote the young prospect, as the big-league club was in the midst of one of their greatest seasons in history, a 109-win romp to the World Series powered by Mantle and Roger Maris. Tresh had a superb year in his own right, hitting .315/.380/.428 in 141 games at shortstop with Richmond and taking home International League MVP honors.
As a reward of sorts, Tresh was tabbed for his MLB debut as a September call-up in ‘61. With another Rookie of the Year-turned-regular in Tony Kubek at shortstop ahead of him, it was hard to find time. Tresh did make it into nine games though, debuting on September 3rd as a pinch-runner and taking his first at-bat on September 16th in his hometown at Tiger Stadium. Tresh notched his first big-league hit in the first game of a doubleheader on September 26th against the Orioles. The huge story that day was Maris tying Babe Ruth with his 60th homer of the season, but Tresh played his part as well, singling to right field off Jack Fisher in the middle of a rally that put the Yankees in front.
Tresh was only technically part of a championship team in ‘61, but the next year, he truly earned his ring. An opportunity arose, as Kubek was recalled to the U.S. Army Reserve. Manager Ralph Houk entrusted the starting role at shortstop to Tresh over fellow infielder Phil Linz. It was the right call, as Tresh went on to an All-Star rookie campaign. He capably fielded the position in Kubek’s absence while hitting well from both sides of the plate. Tresh racked up 20 homers and a .286/.359/.441 triple slash, good for a 119 wRC+, Rookie of the Year honors, and even a 12th-place finish for MVP.
There was the potential for an awkward situation to arise when Kubek returned from the service in August, and Houk tasked Tresh with playing alongside Mantle in left field. In 573 minor-league games, Tresh had never manned the outfield, but he handled it with aplomb. Having previously made that same transition, Mantle even gave Tresh his glove, choosing to befriend and praise his potential future replacement rather than ignoring him, as Joe DiMaggio did to Mantle. Tresh knew Mantle had his flaws, but he loved him anyway and eventually nicknamed his son “Mickey” for him in 1964. (“What the fuck did you do that for?” Mantle later asked. He knew he was no idol.)
The Yankees won the pennant and played the San Francisco Giants in the World Series. Tresh had only just turned 24 and yet he didn’t appear to be fazed at all. He hit .321/.345/.464 in the seven-game series, leading the Yankees in hits and average. It wasn’t garbage time participation either, as his three-run homer in the eighth off Jack Sanford gave the Yankees a Game 5 victory,
Mike Tresh was in the stands at Yankee Stadium when Tresh hit that homer to win Game 5, crying tears of joy. His son had definitely made it.
A terrific one-handed catch by Tresh on a seventh-inning Willie Mays drive in Game 7 likely saved a run with the red-hot Willie McCovey on deck. The Yankees edged the Giants 1-0 to bring home their 20th championship.
Rather than suffering a sophomore slump in ‘63, Tresh had an outstanding year. He was on fire, hitting .269/.371/.487 with 25 dingers and a career-best 141 wRC+. Tresh was an All-Star for the second year in a row and again earned down-ballot MVP votes as the Yankees ran away with the AL pennant thanks to 104 victories. Tresh spent the year in the outfield and even manned center while Mantle missed a few months due to injury. Unfortunately, they had no answer for the overwhelming Los Angeles Dodgers pitching staff in the World Series. Tresh managed to take the seemingly untouchable Sandy Koufax deep late in Game 1, but like most of his team, he was otherwise quiet. They swept the Yankees away.
Houk moved up to the front office in 1964 and the popular Yogi Berra took over in the dugout. The Yankees won their fifth straight pennant, but it was as tough a climb to the top as the team of that era ever endured. They battled injuries and ineffectiveness from several positions, including Kubek at shortstop. Tresh remained a solid player, though he also saw his numbers slip. The Yankees faced a tough competitor in the Cardinals, and it was a tight seven-game series. Tresh slugged .636 and homered twice, including a game-tying blast off World Series MVP Bob Gibson in the ninth inning of Game 5.
It wasn’t enough, as the Cardinals prevailed and Berra was stunningly fired.
The Yankees pulled off a classic “if you can’t beat him, sign him” move for ‘65 by hiring Johnny Keane, who just beat them in the World Series. Kubek played poorly at shortstop and missed a lot of time, but Keane kept Tresh in the outfield, alternating him between relieving Mantle in center and playing left (there was even some right mixed in). To some extent, it paid off, as Tresh finished in the top 10 for AL MVP, won a Gold Glove, and showed no sign of ill-effect at the plate with a 136 wRC+. To another extent, it didn’t, as the team around him was not good; the Yankees fell below .500 for the first time in 40 years.
Despite the increasing effects of a pitching-heavy era, Tresh pulled off a career-high in home runs in ‘66, smacking 27 dingers in 151 games. That was one of the few highlights for the Yankees though, who were abysmal and dropped all the way to last place. Keane was fired and replaced by Houk in May, who moved Tresh to third base since he wanted to give a young Roy White time in the outfield. Tresh ended up splitting time between left and the hot corner. The Yankees appreciated his athleticism and Zobristian ability to handle basically any position, but it still mystified Tresh to a certain degree:
“I win Rookie of the Year as a shortstop and they move me to the outfield. Then I win a Gold Glove Award there in 1965 and they move me to third. I couldn’t figure out what position I was supposed to prove I could play.“
Although Tresh was only 28 entering the 1967 campaign, the second game of spring training was the beginning of the end. He popped his right knee while firing a throw across his body from left field to the cutoff man. Tresh was in serious pain and could barely walk; it was later revealed to be torn cartilage. Inexplicably, the Yankees told him that he should try to play on it rather than undergo surgery.
It was a disaster. Through some miracle, Tresh kept his numbers above league-average with a 106 wRC+, but his OPS dipped below .700 and he was a shadow of the defender he once was in left field. Tresh later recalled that his knee “gave out five more times” that year, undoubtedly affecting his future. He had surgery to repair the damage in the offseason (why he wasn’t simply shut down on a 90-loss team is a mystery), but the damage was done. Tresh was mostly a hobbling shortstop in ‘68 and his play only worsened in ‘69.
By then, the only other position players aside from Tresh remaining from the Yankees’ early ’60s glory were Joe Pepitone and catcher Jake Gibbs. Mantle, Maris, Berra, Kubek, Elston Howard, and Bobby Richardson were all gone. Tresh was miserable. The team was middling at best, and he could barely hit, let alone play shortstop. So he asked if the Yankees would trade him to the Tigers, where he could at least be close to home, not to mention play for the defending World Series champions. The Yankees acquiesced, and Tresh was dealt to Detroit on June 14th. The very next person to wear number 15 for the Yankees was a worthy heir: Thurman Munson.
Tresh remained primarily a shortstop and appeared in 94 games for the Tigers, batting .224/.305/.387 with 13 homers, a .692 OPS that was amusingly still good for a 92 wRC+ in the league-wide offensive malaise. While Detroit was a better team, there was still no competing with the 109-win juggernaut Orioles, who ran away with the AL East in the first year of divisional play.
Tresh had gone through another surgery on his knee in hopes of playing again in 1970. However, the Tigers told him that he would need to rehab in the minors, and Tresh had no intention of living that kind of life again, particularly with a wife and four kids at home. So Tom Tresh retired having played just eight games after his 31st birthday. His story was a warning sign about the dangers of dismissing injuries, but he had no regrets.
Even though Tresh was so talented before his injury that the Red Sox briefly considered a swap of him for Carl Yastrzemski, one can’t blame Tresh for his overall happiness about his career. He was a beloved teammate, a World Series champion, an All-Star, and an MVP candidate for baseball’s greatest franchise. At the time of his retirement, he was even in the Yankees’ all-time top 20 in homers at 140 (the recent offensive spike pushed him back to a tie for 34th as of 2026). Tresh had a fine life post-retirement too, as he did fulfill that college promise to his parents, even after his father’s passing in 1966.
Tresh earned his degree in physical education from Central Michigan in 1969, where he later served as an assistant baseball coach for 15 years and helped innovate a training tool for sliding and diving called the Slide-Rite. His son Mickey inherited the baseball gene, playing at Miami University of Ohio before going through four years in the minors as well with New York and Detroit. The younger Tresh even got a glimpse of the ascendance of one of the great successors to Tresh and Mantle in center: his 1988 Prince William Yankees teammate, 19-year-old Bernie Williams.
The bond between the Mantles and Treshes remained strong—the two Yankees were at a card show in Nashville when Mickey Tresh called to inform his father that he just had a boy of his own, who he named Tommy. Mantle celebrated with Tresh by ordering a $150 bottle of Dom Perignon, raising a toast to the lad, and later writing “Happy birthday Tommy, we had one for you. Mickey Mantle.” on the bottle.
That bottle could have sold for something valuable, as the glove Mantle gave to Tresh in 1962 was enough by itself to put a down payment on a cottage. Tom Tresh never sold it though; it meant too much to him, and he grieved as much as any of his teammates on the day Mantle passed away from liver cancer in 1995. Thirteen years later, Tresh suddenly left the world as well, as he died of a heart attack on October 14, 2008, not even a month after turning 70.
At least Tresh got to see the old Yankee Stadium one last time before it closed for good, as he was in attendance at the final Old-Timers’ Day. As always, the crowd gave him an ovation before he stepped to foul line one last time. Number 15 will always mean Thurman Munson, but it will also always be connected to Tommy Tresh, another fantastic Yankee.

En esta fecha
Pete Rose llegó a 100 hits por vigésimo segundo año consecutivo; Alex Rodríguez completa el 40-40
Albert Pujols estableció récord de carreras impulsadas para un novato de la Liga Nacional; Mariano Rivera impuso una marca de las Grandes Ligas con su salvamento número 602
1968 — Denny McLain ganó su partido número 31, la mayor cantidad en la Liga Americana desde los 31 de Lefty Grove en 1931. Los Detroit Tigers vencieron a los New York Yankees 6-2, mientras que Mickey Mantle conectó su jonrón número 535 y penúltimo de su carrera.
1972 — César Tovar, de Minnesota, completó el ciclo con un jonrón de dos carreras que le dio la victoria a los Twins en la parte baja de la novena entrada, otorgándoles un triunfo de 5-3 sobre los Texas Rangers.
1973 — Frank Robinson conectó su primer jonrón en el Estadio Arlington, como miembro de los California Angels. Fue el trigésimo segundo estadio de las Grandes Ligas en el que conectó un jonrón.
1984 — Pete Rose alcanzó la marca de 100 hits por vigésimo segundo año consecutivo, un récord histórico. También igualó el récord de la Liga Nacional de dobles con 725, cuando los Rojos de Cincinnati vencieron a los Bravos de Atlanta por 4-2.
1986 — Joe Crowley, de los Chicago White Sox, lanzó un juego sin hits ni carreras para guiar a su equipo a una victoria de 7-1 sobre los California Angels.
1995 — Ken Caminiti, de San Diego, se convirtió en el primer jugador en la historia de las Grandes Ligas en conectar jonrones desde ambos lados del plato tres veces en una temporada, al lograr 4 de 4 con un récord personal de ocho carreras impulsadas en una victoria de 15-4 sobre Colorado.
1998 — Alex Rodríguez, de Seattle, conectó su cuadragésimo jonrón para convertirse en el tercer jugador en la historia del béisbol en conectar 40 jonrones y robar 40 bases en la misma temporada.
2001 — Roger Clemens se convirtió en el primer lanzador en la historia de las Grandes Ligas en lograr un récord de 20-1, llevando a los Yankees de Nueva York a una victoria de 6-3 sobre los Medias Blancas de Chicago.
2001 — Albert Pujols estableció un récord de carreras impulsadas para un novato de la Liga Nacional cuando St. Louis venció a Milwaukee 8-2. Pujols impulsó tres carreras para alcanzar las 120 carreras impulsadas, rompiendo la marca de 119 establecida por Wally Berger en 1930 para los Boston Braves.
2008 — El sistema de repetición instantánea del béisbol produjo su primera anulación cuando un doble de dos carreras de Carlos Peña, de Tampa Bay, se convirtió en un jonrón de tres carreras durante la cuarta entrada contra Minnesota.
2008 — Greg Maddox lanza su entrada número 5.000 contra los Gigantes de San Francisco.
2011 — Mariano Rivera estableció un récord de las Grandes Ligas con su salvamento número 602, sellando la victoria de los Yankees de Nueva York por 6-4 sobre los Mellizos de Minnesota.
2017 — Se establece un nuevo récord de la MLB de la mayor cantidad de jonrones en una temporada, 5,694, cuando Alex Gordon de los Kansas City Royals conecta un jonrón.
2024 — Shohei Ohtani irrumpe en un club completamente nuevo del que es el único miembro: el club 50-50. Hoy, logra su primer partido de seis hits, tres de ellos jonrones, sumando 51 en la temporada. También roba dos bases, alcanzando (e incluso superando) la marca de 50, mientras impulsa diez carreras en la aplastante victoria de los Dodgers sobre los Marlins por 20-4. Hace menos de un mes, se convirtió en el sexto miembro del club 40-40, pero ahora se encuentra solo en este nuevo nivel de excelencia sobrenatural, y de paso, ha establecido un nuevo récord de jonrones en una sola temporada para los Dodgers (superando la marca de Shawn Green).

item.content:encoded:
The two most valuable Yankees this season are a starting pitcher named Cam Schlittler, from Walpole, Mass., and Northeastern University, a school within walking distance of Fenway Park, and Ben Rice, who comes out of Cohasset, Mass., on the state’s South Shore, about 30 miles from Fenway. If the Yankees are hosting a Wild Card Series against the Red Sox in less than two weeks -- at Yankee Stadium and not Fenway -- Schlittler and Rice will be the biggest reasons.
Schlittler ought to win the AL Cy Young Award and ought to be an MVP candidate for the whole league. David Cone, now a Yankees broadcaster for the YES network and once a great Yankee himself, has one word to describe what he’s seen from Schlittler this season:
“Nails.”
Here’s a breakdown of Schlittler’s ERA, month by month after one start in March, when, of course, he threw a shutout (eight strikeouts) into the sixth inning against the Giants:
1.73 in April
1.48 in May
3.38 in June
1.93 in July
2.33 in August
0.86 so far in September
Carlos Rodón got hurt. Max Fried got hurt. Gerrit Cole joined the season late, and he hasn’t looked like his own Cy Young self lately. It is been Schlittler who has been the Yankees' ace, who is their Game 1 guy, who has carried the staff. He is not going to end up with a 25-3 record and an ERA of 1.74 the way Ron Guidry did nearly 50 years ago. But Schlittler is at 14-6 with a 1.95 ERA going into his last few starts of the regular season. He has been the first young power starter out of the Yankees’ system since Guidry to be this good, and this dominant.
But Rice has been just as important to their offense.
In a season when Aaron Judge was gone for more than 80 games because of a fracture to his rib cage. Then, after Judge finally got back into the lineup and even hit his first home run in months, he left a game against the Twins the other day because of pain in his lower leg. It is why you have to believe, if and when Judge is back in the lineup again, he’s going to be a swing and a prayer the rest of the way.
So No. 99 went away. So did Cody Bellinger, the Yankees’ second-most important hitter a year ago, before he finally returned from the IL. But even when the Yankees struggled to score runs, and even in a roller-coaster year that saw Rice hit just .196 in June and .184 in August, it is Rice who has been the Yankees' hitting star, coming into a weekend series against the Diamondbacks with 38 home runs and still with a chance to knock in 100.
Luis García Jr. showed up from the Nationals at the Trade Deadline to give him some backup. Bellinger has been on a heater since coming off the IL, with five homers, 18 RBIs and a .344 average over his last 22 games. But it was Rice around whom the Yankees built what offense they had before all that, while they were staying ahead of the Red Sox and at least maintaining contact with the Rays.
You know how many homegrown Yankees have hit 40 or more home runs in a season in the last 75 years? Two. One was named Mickey Mantle and the other is Judge. There have been other Yankees sluggers who got to 40 and beyond. Alex Rodriguez once made it all the way to 57. But they all came from somewhere else. Rice is the same as Schlittler: He hasn’t just come to this moment from New England, he’s someone the Yankees drafted in the 12th round of the 2021 Draft (Schlittler was out of the seventh round the following year).
Alfonso Soriano made his own run at 40 more than 20 years ago. Did it twice. But Soriano came to the Yankees as a free agent from Japan. So think about the company Rice will be keeping if does get to 40 homers, starting with his chance this weekend against the Diamondbacks:
Mantle. Judge.
Here is something Rice’s manager, Aaron Boone, has said about him:
"I got my first taste of him in Spring Training of '24, and it was like, 'Oh, OK.' But then this year, it's gone to even another level.”
Here is something else:
“I think he's turning into one of the best hitters in the league."
Rice himself has predictably low-keyed what he’s done for the Yankees so far.
"The year is still in progress, you know?” he said. “It's still going on. We've got more games to play and a long road ahead, so I can't really look back and assess it fully yet."
It really has been a roller-coaster ride occasionally. He has struggled occasionally against left-handed pitchers, but his season-long average against them stands at .254 with 10 home runs and 29 RBIs.
We know what Schlittler’s numbers are. Rice’s, though, can get a little lost sometimes. But in a year where he’s batted everywhere from leadoff to cleanup, when Judge was gone for more than half the time, he has been indispensable, too. And still has a shot to be a 40-homer guy for the Yankees.

item.content:encoded:
NUEVA YORK — Durante generaciones, el valor de los objetos de colección de Mickey Mantle se ha basado en una combinación ya conocida: el uniforme de los Yankees, su carrera digna del Salón de la Fama y la escasez de los objetos que se conservan de la época de la posguerra en el béisbol.
Pocas piezas tienen tanto valor como la tarjeta Topps de Mantle de 1952. No es su verdadera tarjeta de novato, que pertenece a la colección Bowman de 1951, pero se convirtió en la imagen por excelencia de este icono de los Yankees para los coleccionistas. Un ejemplar en perfecto estado se vendió por 12,6 millones de dólares en 2022, lo que convirtió ese retrato en un símbolo del mercado moderno de objetos de recuerdo deportivos.
La imagen tiene otra faceta que la mayoría de los aficionados de los Yankees nunca ven. Antes de aparecer en el cartón, existía como una fotografía de prensa en blanco y negro tomada durante los entrenamientos de pretemporada de los Yankees en Phoenix. La foto captaba a un Mantle de 19 años antes de su primer partido en las Grandes Ligas y antes de que su nombre se volviera inseparable del Yankee Stadium.
El sistema de clasificación de la PSA ayuda a entender por qué una copia antigua de esa fotografía no se trata como una reproducción normal y corriente. Una fotografía de Tipo I es una copia de primera generación revelada a partir del negativo original en un plazo de unos dos años desde que se tomó la imagen. La PSA afirma que las fotografías de Tipo I suelen ser las más valiosas de sus cuatro categorías fotográficas debido a su antigüedad y originalidad.
La foto de Mantle tiene otro factor que la hace única. La tomó el 5 de marzo de 1951 un fotógrafo no identificado de International News Service y se publicó a nivel regional, no nacional. Esa limitada difusión inicial hizo que quedaran muchas menos copias originales que las innumerables reproducciones posteriores que surgieron tras el ascenso de Mantle con los Yankees.
La distinción es clave. Los coleccionistas no están valorando una impresión conmemorativa posterior ni una copia moderna de la imagen de una tarjeta de los Yankees. Están valorando un objeto de la época que forma parte de la cadena fotográfica que abastecía a los medios de comunicación y que, en última instancia, proporcionó a Topps la base visual para la tarjeta. La procedencia, la generación, el momento y la distribución se dan todos en una misma pieza.
Por qué esta no es solo otra foto más de Mantle
Esa combinación acaba de batir un nuevo récord. Un ejemplar de Tipo I, certificado por la PSA, de la fotografía que se usó para crear el retrato de Mantle de la colección Topps de 1952 se vendió por 3 millones de dólares en una transacción privada gestionada por Hunt Auctions. El coleccionista Ron Firman, de Rye (Nueva York), compró la imagen sin firmar.
Según Henry Yee, experto en autenticación fotográfica de PSA, esta venta supone el precio más alto registrado hasta la fecha por una fotografía de Tipo I. El récord anterior para una fotografía deportiva sin firmar era de 843 750 dólares, pagados en 2024 por una imagen original relacionada con la tarjeta de novato de Mantle de Bowman de 1951.
El récord del mercado fotográfico se dispara casi un 256 %
El nuevo precio es unas 3,56 veces superior al anterior récord de una foto sin firmar. Supera esa cifra en 2 156 250 dólares, lo que supone un aumento de alrededor del 255,6 %. También supera los 1,47 millones de dólares que se pagaron en 2021 por una foto firmada de «Shoeless Joe» Jackson, que por entonces era el récord para una foto deportiva firmada.
Yee señaló que la demanda es una de las razones por las que las fotografías originales de élite se están diferenciando de las fotografías vintage comunes. Su valoración es importante porque el precio de 3 millones de dólares se fijó en una transacción privada, en lugar de en una subasta abierta.
«La demanda de fotografías originales de Tipo I de alta gama por parte de nuevos coleccionistas e inversores que se incorporan al sector está en su punto más alto», afirmó Yee.
También destacó que el material comparable es excepcionalmente escaso, lo que ayuda a explicar por qué una imagen de los Yankees de primera generación puede alcanzar un nivel de precio que normalmente se asocia a las tarjetas de élite.
«Sin embargo, la oferta de este material es extremadamente escasa», dijo Yee.
Un plazo de 43 días hace que la imagen de los Yankees resulte aún más inusual
El momento en que se tomó la foto añade otra razón específica de los Yankees por la que esta imagen es importante. La MLB sitúa el debut de Mantle el 17 de abril de 1951. La foto de Phoenix se tomó 43 días antes, cuando los Yankees aún estaban valorando el potencial de aquel joven promesa de Oklahoma.
Eso significa que la imagen muestra a Mantle antes de que existiera el «resumé». Todavía no había jugado en el Yankee Stadium en ningún partido de las Grandes Ligas, aún no le había quitado el puesto de jardinero central a Joe DiMaggio y no había empezado esa carrera de 18 años con los Yankees en la que consiguió 536 jonrones, tres premios MVP de la Liga Americana y siete títulos de la Serie Mundial.
El Salón de la Fama del Béisbol señala que Mantle jugó toda su carrera con los Yankees, desde 1951 hasta 1968. Ese contexto le da a la foto de marzo de 1951 un carácter diferente al de las fotos publicitarias posteriores. Es un original que se ha conservado de ese breve periodo justo antes de que empezara la leyenda.
La conexión de la tarjeta explica la prima final
La tarjeta de Topps de 1952, la n.º 311, aporta la pieza final del rompecabezas del valor. Topps utilizó esa fotografía como base para el famoso retrato de Mantle que aparece en la tarjeta. La tarjeta se convirtió en uno de los objetos de colección de béisbol más reconocibles de la posguerra, aunque la edición Bowman de 1951 de Mantle es la que se considera su tarjeta de novato.
Para los coleccionistas de los Yankees , esto crea una conexión directa entre los entrenamientos de primavera y uno de los objetos más emblemáticos de este hobby. La fotografía tiene valor por ser una de las primeras imágenes de Mantle, por ser una impresión de Tipo I y porque ese retrato de los Yankees se convirtió en la tarjeta que los coleccionistas llevan décadas buscando.
Hunt Auctions ha dicho que solo se conoce un pequeño número de ejemplares de este tipo I, con autenticación de la PSA. La distribución regional a cargo del International News Service es una de las principales razones de esa escasez.
Por lo tanto, la transacción de 3 millones de dólares refleja algo más que el simple nombre de Mantle. En este objeto se valoran la fuente visual original de la tarjeta, el momento previo a su debut con los Yankees y la rareza de una impresión de primera generación. Esa combinación la sitúa ahora en lo más alto del mercado de la fotografía deportiva.
¿Qué te parece? Deja tu comentario más abajo.

Yahoo Sports: As you likely know by now, Aaron Judge exited yesterday's game early when Heliot Ramos pinch-hit for him in the sixth. The Yankees announced it midgame as "lower leg tightness." It's some relief I suppose that Judge didn't re-aggravate the rib fracture that kept him out for over three months, and Judge himself downplayed the seriousness of the ailment after the game.
"We're still trying to ramp up so there's still going to be little things like this that come up," Judge said after the Yankees 13-inning loss to the Twins. "I just thought it would be best instead of pushing through it like I normally do." Judge seemed to view his exit from the game as precautionary, and likened it to the type of thing that would happen in spring training when small, nagging things pop up as players get back into playing shape.
MLB.com | Patrick Donnelly: Clarke Schmidt came off the 60-day injured list yesterday, something we saw coming; he allowed two hits but got two strikeouts while facing four batters in his first MLB action since July 3, 2025. What we didn't see coming was who was pushed off the roster to make room for Schmidt: fan favorite Oswaldo Cabrera. The utilityman Cabrera had spent most of the year at Triple-A, hitting .288 with 19 homers and a .790 OPS, but hasn't spent much time with the big club ever since suffering a brutal ankle injury in a play at home plate last May. Cabrera seems likely to be claimed on waivers, meaning his time in the Bronx is likely to come to an end after being a member of the organization since signing at age-16 in July 2015.
The Athletic | Brendan Kuty: ($) Spencer Jones has been a bit of a revelation for the Yankees this year, producing at a high level across the outfield throughout the summer. He's benefited from shadowing another big lefty swinger in the outfield: Cody Bellinger. Bellinger is only 31, but has a very long and decorated track record for a player his age, something Jones has tried to tap into during his time with the Yankees. "As a young guy, I can't help but watch every time he's up there," Jones said of Bellinger. "When we are in the dugout," Jones said, "he's one of those people I can go up to and ask, like, 'Yo, what did you see?' He'll tell me bluntly what he saw, how he saw it, and essentially what he's going to do next time."
New York Daily News | Gary Phillips: Ryan Weathers cleared a key hurdle in his rehab earlier this week, tossing 15 pitches in a bullpen session and sitting 87-90 mph on his fastball. The hope, if things go right, is for the lefty to get into game action before the regular season ends. It's a tight timeline, but with Weathers set to throw another bullpen on Friday before perhaps facing live hitters early next week, it's doable. The Yankees could certainly use his arm in the bullpen as they try to sort out what their playoff relief corps will look like.
FanGraphs | Davy Andrews: This here isn't news, but it is fun. Andrews discusses the Amazon TV show Reacher, in which the titular character tries to maintain a low profile by checking into hotels under aliases, which are always Yankees second basemen. The problem, of course, is that Reacher's cover is often blown, because Yankee second basemen are frequently famous people with recognizable names (don't choose "Starlin Castro" as your alias if you're trying not to attract attention!). So, Andrews endeavors to help Reacher by finding players who played second base for the Yankees who would help Reacher stay undercover. Good aliases include second basemen from New York's Higlander days, like Joe Ward, and Otis Johnson. The worst possible aliases Andrews found? Robinson Canó and Mickey Mantle.

item.content:encoded:
In a 1992 Time Magazine profile, Hall-of-Fame broadcaster Bob Costas recalled how his love affair with baseball began. He remembered the cross-country journeys with his dad, twisting the radio dial in his father’s car to pick up broadcasts of MLB games through the crackling static.
“There was a romance to the airwaves,” Costas said, “a notion that moving the dial just slightly enabled you to eavesdrop on what people heard in Baltimore — or, a little farther over, Cincinnati, Philadelphia, and, on a really clear night, St. Louis.”
Costas’ lifelong affinity for America’s pastime was shaped not just by the surpassing greatness of players like Ted Williams, Stan Musial and Mickey Mantle, but by the voices who chronicled their outstanding careers. That star-studded list includes icons such as Jack Buck, Vin Scully, and Ernie Harwell. Each man possessed a distinctive style and a sort of avuncular presence within the organizations for which they worked. Day after day and year after year — through commanding victories and crippling defeats — these golden-throated legends guided baseball fans from spring to autumn.
Their day has long passed, but the relationship between radio listeners and baseball announcers remains. Fans learn to hear, feel and see the game through the vivid descriptions of their favorite voices. Those charismatic raconteurs become a source of comfort — an invitation to withdraw from life’s bustling pace and return to the innocence of childhood. When one of those voices is silenced, the pain is visceral and the loss profound.
New York fans are feeling that loss. John Sterling, who called more than 5,600 Yankees games on radio over 36 years, passed away Monday at the age of 87. Yankees TV broadcaster Michael Kay, who shared the radio booth with Sterling for much of the 1990s, spoke with Sports Media Watch about his longtime colleague.
“He is as significant and relevant as many Yankee players throughout history,” said Kay. “Broadcasters are here sometimes a lot longer than players, and they become part of the fabric and part of the family of the people that listen. For 36 years, he was everybody’s friend every summer, so I think he leaves an incredible legacy. In this age of digital retention of everything that’s said and done, his calls are going to live forever. He happened to broadcast during a time when the Yankees did a lot of winning and won five championships, so his voice is going to be just as significant as Mel Allen’s.”
In the days following his passing, a litany of current and former players, sports media personalities and Yankee fans have paid tribute to the man nicknamed “Pa Pinstripe.” During a segment on his radio show this week, ESPN host and longtime Yankees fan Rich Eisen called Sterling “a companion.”
Was he polarizing? Yes. Could he be bombastic? Yes. Were his custom home run calls (an A Bomb … from A-Rod!) hammy and over the top? Sure. But Sterling’s style didn’t have to be met with every fan’s approval. If you weren’t an ardent Yankee devotee, John Sterling’s performative presentation was likely not your cup of tea.
Yet it is important to remember where Sterling’s loyalties lay. He didn’t just work for the Yankees; he belonged to the Yankees. And as the Bronx Bombers dominated the back half of the 1990s, Sterling’s enthusiastic “Yankees win! THUUUUUHHHH Yankees WIN!” became a familiar refrain.
Television has always been the glitzier medium for play-by-play, but its gaudiness produces a certain distance between the announcer and the viewer. Radio is the purer, less pretentious medium, breaking down the barriers and creating an atmosphere of intimacy, where the listener leans in on every word picture the announcer paints. Every noun, every adjective, every verb becomes a tool the commentator uses to paint his/her own 9-inning masterpiece.
John Sterling knew he was a different kind of artist, one whose colors were louder and more vibrant than most. But his lengthy career and the undeniable connection he developed with a loving fanbase is a testament to the power of baseball radio play-by-play and its uncanny ability to unite and bind generations of avid followers.
Plus: Taylor does her best work in NBC’s NBA studio
Since 2021, Maria Taylor has served as one of NBC’s most prominent anchors, ably handling college football, NFL, and Olympic hosting duties for the network. Yet over the last 7 months, the role of lead NBA studio host has proven to be the assignment with which she is most comfortable.
It was an obvious choice for NBC Sports. Taylor played basketball for her alma mater the University of Georgia, and, for a few years, she was ESPN’s lead NBA anchor before her controversial departure from the company.
Despite the network’s belief in Taylor’s talents, NBC’s studio show “NBA Showtime” presented real challenges. Hall of Famers Carmelo Anthony, Tracy McGrady, and Vince Carter bring elite playing experience, but are still developing in their roles as full-time television analysts, placing greater responsibility on Taylor to steer and enliven conversations, plus ensure her analysts make certain needful observations.
In this area, Taylor has excelled. Discussions are free-flowing, creating a light, relaxed and friendly atmosphere. Simply put, it feels like Taylor, Anthony, Carter and McGrady genuinely get along. And in television, that’s half the battle.
No one can credibly argue that the Showtime cast is as entertaining as the “Inside the NBA” quartet of EJ, Shaq, Kenny and Chuck but, with Taylor’s lighthearted guidance, they do just enough to keep fans engaged.
Viewers can tell when a host likes the sport they cover. There’s a certain glint in their eyes, a certain ease that translates well on camera. “Football Night in America” is her highest profile role, but on “NBA Showtime,” viewers get Maria Taylor at her best.

item.content:encoded:
Collectors have spent decades paying increasingly ridiculous amounts of money for Mickey Mantle’s iconic 1952 Topps card, so apparently the hobby eventually had to work backward to the thing that existed before the cardboard. The original photograph Topps used to create the card’s famous image just sold privately for $3 million.
The 7-by-9-inch black-and-white photograph was taken during Yankees spring training in Phoenix on March 5, 1951, months before Mantle made his major-league debut. Hunt Auctions brokered the private transaction, with Sports Collectors Daily reporting the price established a record for a Type I sports photograph.
The Cardboard Is Not Even The Most Interesting Part Anymore
This was basically the raw material for one of the most recognizable baseball cards ever made.
International News Service originally distributed the photo regionally rather than nationally, which helped make surviving originals extremely scarce. Topps later used Mantle’s portrait as the basis for the painted image on card No. 311 in its 1952 set.
The photograph carries PSA’s coveted Type I classification, which means it was developed from the original negative within roughly two years of the image being taken. PSA considers Type I examples the most desirable category because they are first-generation photographs created closest to the moment itself.
Only a handful of Type I versions of this particular Mantle image are known, which apparently makes $3 million sound reasonable to somebody.
The same kind of photograph sold for $375,000 in 2019. Another Type I image, the photograph used for his actual 1951 Bowman rookie card, sold for $843,750 in 2024, which made it the most expensive one ever sold in the category.
Now the 1952 Topps source photo has essentially taken that market and launched it into another tax bracket.
The Buyer Also Owns A $12.6 Million Card
Here is where this turns from expensive collecting into assembling the world’s most ridiculous before-and-after set.
The buyer was commercial real-estate investor Ron Firman, who also owns the famous SGC Mint+ 9.5 example of the 1952 Topps Mantle that Heritage sold for $12.6 million in 2022.
So one collector now owns both the photograph and the cardboard masterpiece it helped create. Combined purchase price: $15.6 million.
There is also a funny distinction worth making whenever the 1952 Mantle comes up. Despite frequently being called a rookie card, Mantle’s recognized rookie was issued by Bowman in 1951. The 1952 version was his first Topps card and simply became so famous that it eventually swallowed almost everything else connected to his collecting market.
Now even the source material is worth more than most pieces of luxury real estate.

item.content:encoded:
The most iconic Mickey Mantle image fetched an insane price.
Ron Firman of Rye, N.Y., purchased for $3 million the first edition of the non-autographed, PSA-authenticated photo of the iconic Yankees center fielder that later became Mantle’s legendary 1952 Topps card.
The picture of Mantle was sold at a private sale brokered by Hunt Auctions.
It is a PSA Type 1 photo, meaning it is a “first-generation photograph, developed from the original negative, during the period (within approximately two years of when the picture was taken),” according to psacard.com.
That picture was taken by an unknown International News Service photographer at Yankees spring training in Phoenix on March 5, 1951, though the photographer carried no credit so it’s unclear if the individual was a company staffer or a freelancer.
“The demand for high-end original Type I photographs from new collectors and investors coming into the space is at an all-time high,” said PSA photo authenticator Henry Yee.
“The supply, however, for this material is extremely scarce. When an item of this caliber is offered for sale, often it is sold privately and does not even make it to public auction — such as in this case.”
Highly graded copies of Mantle’s iconic 1952 Topps card have fetched obscene prices at auction, including a record $12.6 million in August 2022.
That 1952 card is not his rookie card, though.
Mantle’s rookie card is from Bowman’s 1951 set, which has sold for as much as $843,750, though that card is not a real picture but a painted image.
The 1952 Topps card is a real image on cardboard and one of the most famous images in all of sports memorabilia.
In PSA’s pool, there are only 2,075 copies of Mantle’s 1952 Topps card across all grades.
Mantle played for the Yankees from 1951-66 and authored one of baseball’s most legendary careers, primarily manning center field as a left-handed-swinging power hitter from Oklahoma.
He tallied 536 homers, but his body began to fall apart after the 1961 home run chase with Roger Maris, when Mantle hit 54 home runs and drove in 128 runs, while Maris hit a then-record 61 homers and drove in 141.

item.content:encoded:
Baseball Hall of Fame pitcher and legendary New York Yankees starter CC Sabathia has told the story many times: Dave Stewart changed his mindset forever at just 9 years old in his hometown Vallejo, California.
Stewart, a three-time World Series champion and World Series MVP during his time pitching for the Oakland Athletics, made a surprise visit to Sabathia’s Boys and Girls Club when he was just a kid. Stewart shared a message of inspiration, and it’s one that stuck with a fellow African American major league great who just so happened to hoist his own World Series trophy in a town known best for their hardware on the diamond.
It’s hard to become a Yankees legend, and it’s even harder to find your name amongst the rarest of rare in Monument Park, where the likes of Mickey Mantle, Babe Ruth and Lou Gehrig reside in immortality. On Sept. 26, Sabathia will have his No. 52 retired forever by one of the most iconic franchises in sports, an honor he can’t wait to finally see come to life after learning the shocking news months prior.
But while Sabathia’s on-field accomplishments are Hall of Fame and Monument Park worthy, his off-the-field contributions to the next generation are just as timeless and important.
That was on full display Monday at Alpine Country Club in New Jersey, where Sabathia held his 6th Annual Golf Classic for his PitCCh In Foundation. With golf being his latest sports passion post-retirement, it’s a day Sabathia looks forward to with his friends while making a community impact that feels as good as hitting a hole-in-one.
"It’s always fun to be able to get out on the golf course and obviously raise money for a good cause," he told FOX Business before teeing off alongside the likes of Victor Cruz, Gary Sheffield, JR Smith, Matt Barnes, Ron Harper, Jimmy Rollins, Ja Rule and the list goes on. "Our foundation, the money goes directly to the kids in the Bronx. Our kids back home in our hometown of Vallejo [California], this is a direct effect of people coming out here to play golf.
"I was just sitting down talking to Adam Jones and talking about being able to play golf, and the last six years, the network I’ve been able to build just around the game of golf. I wish I would’ve been playing longer, but I’m here now and excited."
The event raised more than $450,000 to help PitCCh In continue creating opportunities and resources for young people and their families on both coasts in one unforgettable day.
It’s moments like this that have Sabathia excited for this next chapter of his life. Yes, he will still be impacting the game of baseball, whether that be broadcasting, or working with the Yankees and MLB as a whole.
But his foundation is something he holds near and dear to his heart, as does his wife Amber and their four children. In fact, PitCCh In is a true part of the family in their eyes.
"It’s great to see the foundation thriving in retirement. Sometimes in retirement, foundations go by the wayside, or players get busy and different things happen. But this is kind of our fifth child we’ve always said," he said, smiling. "PitCCh In has been such a huge part of not just our lives, but like we said, kids on both coasts [and] our kids’ lives.
"I was just with Derek [Jeter] and he celebrated his 30 years for Turn 2 [Foundation], and just the impact he’s been able to make on the youth just in general. So many different stories, Jeter’s Leaders [Program] and people, in the last 30 years that he’s been able to impact. Hopefully, PitCCh In can continue to be that vehicle for years to come, too."
PitCCh In has done everything from field renovations to baseball clinics, to providing college scholarships and school supplies as ways to impact the communities the Sabathia family cares about most. They also have a mentorship program where, through educational and athletic activities, the lives of the youth involved are strengthened on levels both physical and emotional.
Sabathia’s baseball legacy will be told forever in the halls in Cooperstown and behind the center field wall at Yankee Stadium come Sept. 26. But his story is one that goes well beyond the baseball player.
It’s also the person he is, and the family he’s surrounded by, that continues to support and impact in a way he felt from the very beginning.
"It was big for me when I was a kid, just having people that took interest in my life," he said. "I just think about me being lucky in the situation I was in, whether it was my Boys and Girls Club – there was a guy named Philmore Graham who ran my Boys and Girls Club and took a huge interest in me. My high school baseball coach, my fifth grade teacher, all these different people who made an impact and why I’m sitting here. I want to hopefully be that for a kid."

item.content:encoded:
MINNEAPOLIS — George Lombard Jr. se encontraba en medio de la última celebración de los Yankees el lunes por la noche, con la cerveza chorreándole por la gorra y tras haber dado uno de los golpes más importantes de su joven carrera.
El novato campocorto abrió la octava entrada en el Target Field con un doble ante Andrew Morris, mandando una bola rápida de 98 mph hacia el centro-izquierdo cuando los Yankees iban perdiendo 2-1 ante los Minnesota Twins. A eso le siguieron seis carreras. Aaron Judge conectó el jonrón de tres carreras que sentenció el partido, y Nueva York se llevó la victoria por 8-3, asegurándose así otro viaje a octubre.
Tim Hill se llevó la victoria, Morris cargó con la derrota y John Schreiber se anotó el salvamento. Los Yankees mejoraron su balance a 87-63 y se colocaron a 3,5 partidos de Tampa Bay en la División Este de la Liga Americana.
Los Yankees le han pedido a un novato de 21 años que aprenda a jugar en la posición del cuadro más exigente de la organización en plena lucha por el título. En su debut en las Grandes Ligas, conectó un jonrón y brilló en defensa. Unas semanas más tarde, cometió un error en seis partidos seguidos y sufrió un bajón ofensivo que puso a prueba su capacidad de adaptación.
El lunes volvió a mostrar su otra cara. Lombard se fue con 1 de 4, anotó la carrera del empate y ayudó a encender la remontada que llevó a los Yankees a la postemporada por novena vez en diez temporadas. Ese hit le dejó con un total de 24 de 110, un promedio de .218, con tres jonrones y 11 carreras impulsadas.
Quizá la pregunta más importante para los Yankees sea cómo aprenderá Lombard a lidiar con todo lo que conlleva este puesto antes de que octubre le ponga aún más en el punto de mira.
Esa presión ya es una realidad. Los Yankees ven a Lombard como parte del equipo actual, no solo como una promesa a la que le dan minutos de juego en septiembre, y cada error o cada avance tiene ahora consecuencias en partidos que cuentan.
Una conversación de enero que ahora se ve de otra manera
Meses antes de que Lombard supiera que iba a ser el shortstop titular de los Yankees, se sentó a desayunar en Miami con Derek Jeter.
La cita la organizó un amigo común, según Brendan Kuty, de The Athletic, que dio a conocer los detalles el martes. Lombard se estaba preparando para los entrenamientos de primavera y iba a empezar la temporada en la Doble A.
Kuty destacó el doble del lunes como otra muestra de por qué los Yankees siguen apostando por el potencial de Lombard.
«Fue una demostración de ese talento natural para batear que hace que los Yankees tengan tan buena opinión de Lombard», escribió Kuty.
Pero lo más revelador de la reunión no tuvo mucho que ver con batear. Lombard dijo que la conversación versó sobre la vida con los Yankees, los medios de comunicación, las exigencias fuera del campo y la responsabilidad que conlleva ser una figura tan conocida en Nueva York.
«En Nueva York, el rendimiento en el campo es súper importante», dijo Lombard. «Pero tu carácter y cómo eres como persona son igual de importantes».
Ese mensaje ha cobrado más relevancia de lo que ninguno de los dos jugadores podría haber imaginado en enero.
Una prueba de resistencia de 42 días da un nuevo peso a la lección de Jeter
Solo 42 días separaron el debut de Lombard, el 4 de agosto, del 15 de septiembre. En ese tiempo, 32 partidos de las Grandes Ligas ya han traído consigo ese tipo de altibajos que pueden marcar la diferencia en la temporada de un novato en Nueva York.
Lombard empezó el 2026 en la Doble A, fue subiendo hasta la Triple A y llegó a los Yankees el 4 de agosto. Con 21 años y 63 días, se convirtió en el jugador más joven de los Yankees en ser titular como campocorto desde Jeter, que tenía 20 años y 350 días cuando fue titular en esa posición el 11 de junio de 1995.
Los Yankees no te lo pusieron fácil a Lombard para entrar en la plantilla. Le dieron el puesto de campo corto justo en plena lucha por los playoffs.
Bateó un jonrón en su debut. El 9 de septiembre, conectó el primer grand slam de los Yankees de la temporada y se convirtió en el jugador más joven de los Yankees en batear uno desde Mickey Mantle. El lunes, tras otra racha complicada al bate, conectó el doble que dio inicio a la entrada decisiva en Minnesota.
Su rendimiento irregular sigue formando parte de la evaluación. Al comenzar el lunes, Lombard tenía un promedio de .215, un OPS de .619 y un wRC+ de 73. En defensa ha demostrado la potencia de brazo y el alcance que lo convirtieron en el mejor prospecto de la organización, pero su racha de seis partidos con errores puso de manifiesto lo implacable que puede ser esa posición.
Ahí es donde la comparación con Jeter cobra importancia. Los Yankees están viendo cómo responde Lombard cuando el éxito, el fracaso y la atención llegan casi al mismo tiempo.
Boone ve algo más allá de los consejos sobre béisbol
Aaron Boone vio la decisión de Lombard de acudir a Jeter como una muestra de la curiosidad del novato por la franquicia y por su puesto.
El entrenador le dijo a The Athletic que valora a los jugadores que quieren entender la historia y la importancia de la organización de los Yankees. Lombard no buscó a Jeter solo para que le diera consejos técnicos. Quería saber cómo se las apañaba Jeter en la propia ciudad de Nueva York.
«Me encanta cuando a nuestros jugadores les interesa sentirse parte de la organización», dijo el entrenador de los Yankees. «Hacer algo así e ir a hablar con Derek… son cosas geniales, cuando tus jugadores muestran curiosidad. Mira, no todo el mundo es así. Hay que respetarlo. Pero te encanta cuando los chicos sienten curiosidad, entienden la importancia de esta organización y quieren formar parte importante de ella».
Aun así, Lombard dijo que la reunión con Jeter le pareció diferente. Las preguntas más importantes giraron en torno a cómo lidiar con el revuelo que rodeaba al partido.
El segundo mensaje de Jeter llega con el final de octubre
La relación no se quedó solo en el desayuno.
Jeter volvió al Yankee Stadium el viernes para los actos que conmemoraban el 25.º aniversario del 11 de septiembre. Visitó el vestuario de los Yankees y volvió a encontrarse con Lombard, que ya no era un joven promesa que soñaba con el puesto, sino el novato que lo ocupaba.
Lombard dijo que Jeter se alegró por él y le dio otro mensaje conciso.
«Ha sido un año un poco de locos», dijo Lombard. «Pero él se alegra por mí y me ha dicho que siga a lo mío y que no pierda la concentración».
Los Yankees ya se han asegurado una plaza en la postemporada, pero Lombard sigue aprendiendo mientras el equipo persigue a Tampa Bay por el título de la división. Su bate aún tiene que mejorar. En defensa, puede pasar de estar impecable a cometer errores costosos.
Jeter no puede hacer esos ajustes por él. Lo que le ofreció a Lombard fue un marco de referencia para desenvolverse en esa posición mientras los va haciendo.
Para los Yankees, eso puede ser tan importante como cualquier cambio en el swing que el novato haga antes de octubre.
¿Qué le parece? Deje su comentario a continuación.

item.content:encoded:
PCA began the day with 9.8 Wins Above Replacement (WAR) according to the formula used at FanGraphs, which is also referred to as fWAR. After a huge, four-hit performance, which included his 42nd home run and 37th stolen base in a 7-3 Cubs win over the Braves, PCA climbed over the 10-WAR line, finishing at 10.1. That is blowing away the field and then some. Shohei Ohtani ranks second in the Majors at 6.8 fWAR, and that includes both his batting and pitching value.
The 3.3-WAR gap between Crow-Armstrong and Ohtani equals the gap between Ohtani and the duo of Jake Bauers and Bryce Harper, who are tied for 60th in MLB. If that holds, it would be the first time in 70 years that there was a 3-fWAR gap between the No. 1 and No. 2 players -- since Mickey Mantle (11.5) finished well ahead of Duke Snider (7.5) in 1956. The only other players in the Modern Era (since 1900) to lead by at least 3 fWAR are Rogers Hornsby (1925, '29) and Babe Ruth (1919, '20, '23, '26).
Now, before we go any further, let’s acknowledge two points:
- WAR can go both up and down, so PCA’s might theoretically drop back under 10. (He already did once, after briefly getting to exactly 10.0.)
- There are two major versions of WAR, one at FanGraphs and one at Baseball-Reference (also referred to as bWAR). These systems use somewhat different inputs and calculate WAR differently, so while they generally are in the same ballpark, they don’t line up exactly. In Crow-Armstrong’s case, he still leads the Majors in bWAR, but with “only” 9.3 entering Tuesday, or 1.7 ahead of Phillies pitcher Cristopher Sánchez.
A 10-WAR season by both models is still in play for Crow-Armstrong, if hardly guaranteed, with 11 games remaining. But even reaching that plateau via one of the two systems is quite an accomplishment. For PCA, it comes down to being great across the board. (All numbers via FanGraphs, entering Tuesday.)
- His 157 wRC+ (compared to the park-adjusted league average of 100) ranks second in the Majors among qualifiers, behind only Yordan Alvarez.
- His 6.9 baserunning runs above average, which factors in both his stolen bases and general success on the bases, ranks fifth in MLB.
- Because he plays a difficult, up-the-middle position and excels at it, his defensive value is the best in baseball, edging out Royals shortstop Bobby Witt Jr.
While PCA’s final total will be decided between now and Sept. 27, let’s take a closer look at the company he would be keeping, assuming he maintains his place in the 10-WAR club.
Note: We’re looking at total WAR here, as opposed to just hitting or pitching WAR. Total WAR combines offensive, defensive and pitching value, which affects not just Ohtani, but also pitchers who hit prior to the universal DH or even position players who have made rare pitching appearances.
Players with 10-WAR seasons in the 30-team era (since 1998)
Aaron Judge
2025 (10.0 fWAR), 2024 (11.2 fWAR, 10.9 bWAR), 2022 (11.1 fWAR, 10.8 bWAR)
Judge missed large chunks of 2023 and ‘26 to injury, but he notched 10 WAR via at least one of the two systems in three consecutive full seasons. In each of the three, he posted a wRC+ of over 200, or more than twice the league average.
Bobby Witt Jr.
2024 (10.5 fWAR)
Witt was the epitome of a complete player in 2024. He posted his second straight 30-30 season, led all MLB hitters with a .332 average and 211 hits, had a 170 wRC+, won his first Gold Glove with an AL-best 16 Outs Above Average at shortstop, and finished second in the AL MVP vote.
Mookie Betts
2018 (10.2 fWAR, 10.7 bWAR)
Betts’ 2018 campaign was the peak of a five-year period from 2015-19 in which he averaged 8.1 bWAR per season. He led MLB with a .346 average and .640 slugging percentage, hit 32 homers and had a 185 wRC+ on his way to AL MVP honors with the world champion Red Sox.
Mike Trout
2016 (10.4 bWAR), 2013 (10.1 fWAR), 2012 (10.1 fWAR, 10.5 bWAR)
Peak Trout had many thinking he could end up being the best player of all time, and his three 10 WAR seasons represented the peak of the peak. Those seasons resulted in the 2012 AL Rookie of the Year Award, the 2016 AL MVP and a wRC+ low of 167.
Zack Greinke
2009 (10.4 bWAR)
No pitcher has crossed the 10-WAR threshold since Greinke did so with the Royals in 2009. He pitched to a 2.16 ERA in 33 starts across 229 1/3 innings on his way to his first – and only – career Cy Young Award.
Barry Bonds
2004 (11.9 fWAR, 10.6 bWAR), 2003 (10.2 fWAR), 2002 (12.7 fWAR, 11.7 bWAR), 2001 (12.5 fWAR, 11.8 bWAR)
From 2001-04, a period in which he was named NL MVP each year, Bonds was quite possibly the most feared hitter who ever lived. In ’01, he set the single-season home run record by smashing 73, and from 2002-04, he broke and re-broke the all-time single-season mark for intentional walks -- he set a record with 68 in ’02, then was issued an intentional free pass 61 times in ’03 and an unfathomable 120 times in ’04. Even prior to that historic run, Bonds produced 9-plus WAR four times (1990, ’92, ’93 and ’96).
Alex Rodriguez
2002 (10.0 fWAR), 2000 (10.4 bWAR)
A-Rod had one of the greatest walk years in MLB history in 2000, when he posted a 1.026 OPS with 41 home runs and 132 RBIs for the Mariners just before inking a then-record 10-year, $252 million contract with the Rangers. Two years later, he belted a career-best 57 home runs to go along with an MLB-leading 142 RBIs and 389 total bases for Texas.
Randy Johnson
2002 (10.5 bWAR)
The Hall of Fame left-hander won four consecutive NL Cy Young Awards with the D-backs from 1999 to 2002, averaging 9.5 WAR per season. Johnson was most dominant in the final year of that stretch, going 24-5 with a 2.32 ERA (195 ERA+, or 95% better than league average) and 334 strikeouts in 260 innings.
Sammy Sosa
2001 (10.2 bWAR)
Slammin’ Sammy Sosa won the NL MVP Award behind a 66-home run barrage in 1998. But his best season may have actually occurred three years later. In 2001, Sosa posted a 186 wRC+, or production 86% better than league average, behind 64 home runs and 160 RBIs.
Pedro Martinez
2000 (11.7 bWAR), 1999 (11.6 fWAR)
Martinez was quite good in his first season with the Red Sox in 1998, finishing as the runner-up in AL Cy Young Award voting. But that was just an appetizer for the dominance that followed. Martinez won consecutive Cy Young Awards in 1999 and 2000, each time leading the Majors in ERA and the AL in strikeouts.
Kevin Brown
1998 (10.0 fWAR)
Brown was a workhorse for the Marlins, Padres and Dodgers from 1996-2000, and the ’98 campaign -- his lone season with San Diego -- was his finest over that span. The hard-throwing right-hander finished that season with a 2.38 ERA (2.23 FIP) and 5.2 strikeout-to-walk ratio over 257 innings for the NL champions.

item.content:encoded:
Artwork
Type 1 photo with image used for 1952 Topps Mickey Mantle card sells for record $3M
There’s no slowing down the Mickey Mantle market.
Top-notch examples of the New York Yankees star’s iconic 1952 Topps card have been selling for seven figures for a number of years. Each graded copy continues to increase in value.
Now, the original black-and-white photograph with the image used for his first-ever Topps card is joining the million dollar Mantle club.
Hunt Auctions announced that it brokered the sale of a rare Mantle Type I photo for $3 million through a private deal. That is an all-time record sale for a PSA-authenticated Type I photograph.
“This is huge for the photo collecting community, because it’s such a big number,” Henry Yee, principal authenticator for PSA Photo Authentication Services, told SCD. “When you talk about any collectible that crosses $1 million, whether it be tickets or magazines, it’s huge. Actually, photos have crossed $1 million but they were private sales.”
Related Content:
The previous record sale for an unsigned Type I original photograph was $843,750 on April 7, 2024 through Heritage Auctions. That was also a Mantle photo, which became the image used for his 1951 Bowman rookie card.
“The 1952 Topps Mickey Mantle rookie card remains to date one of the most recognizable American sports and popular culture items of the last 100 years,” said David Hunt, president of Hunt Auctions. “The record-setting price achieved for the related photograph is one of scant few PSA/DNA Type I examples known to exist and is among the most coveted original sports images of any type. This astounding record-setting image further memorializes the elite status of the Topps Mickey Mantle rookie card within the history of American popular culture. We are honored to have facilitated this historic sale, which undoubtedly has established a pricing standard of great significance.”
The Type I Mantle photograph was purchased by Hunt Auctions on behalf of prominent sports memorabilia collector Ron Firman.
“Mickey Mantle was a great player who was universally admired,” said Firman, who became a baseball fan growing up in a New York City suburb. “Our love for sports and its heroes help bring us together in our communities and as a nation, and that’s very important.
“I really want to thank Dave Hunt of Hunt Auctions for his valued assistance in this process and expertise within the market.”
PHOTO CLASSIFICATION
Type I photos, which are first-generation photos that were developed from the original negative within two years of the image being taken, are rare in general. They are also the most valuable and coveted photos by collectors.
PSA has only authenticated three Type I copies of the famous Mantle photograph with the image that Topps ended up using for its 1952 set. Yee has authenticated all three during his tenure at PSA.
In 2005, Yee along with legendary collector Marshall Fogel and Khyber Oser wrote a book titled “A Portrait of Baseball Photography.” The authors created a classification system, labeling photos Type I, II, III or IV, depending on when images were developed.
“Original Type Is are made off of the original negative in a dark room,” Yee said. “It’s as clean as it gets. It’s the most valuable of an image. It’s right off the negative.”
Fogel is a big Type I photograph collector. He knows the importance of this Mantle sale to the entire photography segment of the hobby.
“In a little over 25 years, the value of Type I photos, as evidenced by this sale, have increased exponentially,” Fogel told SCD. “The reason is two-fold: one is the preservation of nostalgia in knowing that this kind of photography, especially the news service photography, is extremely valuable because it’s very limited—including Types II, III and IV. The second is people are starting to realize the importance of the content of these photos. The preservation of our history from the beginning of the early days of baseball in the era of Ty Cobb, Christy Mathewson, Walter Johnson on through the era of Mickey Mantle, Sandy Koufax and Joe DiMaggio. It represents the golden ages of baseball history.”
MANTLE CARD SALES
Prior to this latest sale, the owner of the Type I Mantle photograph wasn’t planning on moving the item.
However, when a PSA 8 example of Mantle’s 1952 Topps card sold for $3.721 million through Heritage Auctions on Aug. 23, that pushed the photograph owner to let go of his prized piece.
The 7-by-9-inch Mantle photograph was taken by a photographer who was either an employee or freelancer—it is not known—for the International News Service (INS). The picture was snapped 75 years ago on March 5, 1951 during a Yankees’ spring training photo shoot.
With Mantle being an almost unknown 19-year-old rookie, having the photographer take his picture was almost an afterthought. However, the image became iconic, and not many original copies of the photograph survived at news services.
“A lot of these photos, they’re valuable simply because they weren’t meant to be collected,” Yee said. “They were basically a byproduct of an industry, and that industry was basically reporting the news of the day. They were made in small quantities. They were sent to various news payrolls of an agency.”
The Mantle Type I photo that just sold was originally discovered in 2012. Legendary Auctions president and COO Doug Allen found the piece in the archives of a regional U.S. newspaper. The back of the photo is plastered with writing. It contains an “International News Photo” stamp, along with stamps from at least five dates that signify the photo was used by the news publication.
After the Type I photo was authenticated and encapsulated by PSA/DNA in 2012, Legendary Auctions sold the photograph for $59,750.
“At the time when this sold for $59,000, that was a massive record price,” Yee said. “At that time, I’m not sure even PSA 8s of Mantle’s Topps rookie card sold for $59,000.
“It kind of mirrors what the PSA 8 goes for, it seems like.”
In November 2019, one of the two other Type I Mantle photographs that exist—stamped on the back with “Newark Sunday News” and with a chipped corner on the upper right—sold for $375,000. Purchased by a private collector, that was a record price at the time.
“This one is probably distinguished by the editorial markings on the middle right side,” said Yee, noting the third Mantle Type I photo is also part of a private collection.
COVETED TYPE 1 PHOTOS
The Mantle photo with the image used for his 1952 Topps card is one of the most coveted Type I photos in the hobby. According to Yee, the holy grail for Type I photos is of Honus Wagner. The shot was taken by Carl Horner in 1902 and later used for his famous 1909-11 T206 card.
Fogel owns the only example of the Wagner photograph. Yee said if that piece was ever sold, it would probably fetch eight figures.
“The Mantle is considered the modern grail, just like it mirrors cards, where you’ve got the Wagner T206 is the pre-war grail and the ’52 Topps Mantle would be the post-war grail,” Yee said.
The Mantle sale not only increases the values for Mantle Type I photos but it benefits every Type I photo across the board.
“With photos, it’s unique in a sense that it’s kind of like art. It’s not really like cards where you have Card Ladder or a VCP,” Yee said. “People that have Mantle cards, they’re going to ask for more now—that I’m certain of. This will definitely bump and will probably even bump the low-end stuff. When people hear of something like this, they think, ‘You know what, maybe I should pick up a Type I Mantle or a Type I Clemente, just to have and ride the wave.’ It’s like that in every segment of the market.”

item.content:encoded:
MINNEAPOLIS — El champán aún goteaba de las lonas de plástico cuando George Lombard Jr. saboreó por primera vez aquello a lo que había aspirado toda su vida. El lunes por la noche, en el vestuario de visitantes del Target Field, empapado de champán, este novato de 21 años celebró su primera clasificación para la postemporada en su carrera en las Grandes Ligas.
Se había ganado su puesto en el equipo. Lombard ayudó a dar el empujón definitivo que sentenció el partido, y durante unas horas se mostró tal y como los Yankees se lo imaginaban en octubre cuando ascendieron a su mejor promesa en agosto.
Los Yankees vencieron a los Twins por 8-3 y así hicieron oficial la celebración. La derrota anterior de Toronto ante Detroit ya les había asegurado matemáticamente la clasificación, pero la remontada de Nueva York garantizó que la clasificación llegara con una victoria, en lugar de con un simple encogimiento de hombros mientras miraban el marcador.
Para Lombard, fue el tipo de noche que justifica un ascenso meteórico. Apenas lleva un mes en las grandes ligas y ya tiene una celebración por el título en su haber. La euforia, sin embargo, no duró toda la noche.
Lombard enciende la mecha en la octava
Los Yankees iban perdiendo 2-1 al comenzar la octava y apenas habían hecho nada contra el pitcheo de Minnesota durante siete entradas. Lombard cambió el rumbo con un solo swing, abriendo la entrada con un doble que colocó a la carrera del empate en posición de anotar.
Por fin, la alineación se despertó detrás de él. José Caballero conectó un sencillo que llevó a Lombard a home y empató el partido; después, Anthony Volpe y Caballero lograron un doble robo. Ben Rice conectó un sencillo con el bate roto que impulsó dos carreras, y Cody Bellinger siguió con otro sencillo.
Aaron Judge dio el golpe de gracia. El capitán conectó un jonrón de tres carreras de 415 pies, su aportación a una entrada de seis carreras que convirtió un 2-1 en contra en una ventaja de 7-2. Austin Wells añadió un jonrón solitario en la novena, y los Yankees mejoraron su balance a 87-63.
Lombard estaba al frente de todo eso. Esa es exactamente la situación que se imaginaban los Yankees cuando le dieron el puesto de campocorto a una promesa que apenas había jugado en las ligas menores superiores. Su bate, que antes era una incógnita, no deja de dar respuestas.
«Ha sido genial», dijo tras la victoria. «Obviamente, fue un momento clave del partido y hice todo lo que pude para llegar a base en esa jugada».
El error que empañó la celebración
Entonces llegó el giro inesperado que impidió que la noche fuera un triunfo rotundo. Más adelante en el partido, Lombard cometió otro error, una nueva entrada en un historial defensivo que se ha alargado demasiado para un jugador cuyo guante se suponía que era su punto fuerte.
El momento fue un golpe duro. Justo la noche en que los Yankees se aseguraron el título, su shortstop novato les volvió a recordar el único punto débil que podría ser clave cuando cambie el año. Ese contraste —un gran impacto ofensivo seguido de un fallo defensivo— se ha convertido en la tónica dominante de su joven carrera.
No se suponía que fuera así. Cuando los Yankees ascendieron a Lombard, los ojeadores consideraban que su defensa era la parte más sólida de su juego. En cambio, los errores se han ido acumulando de una forma que casi nadie había previsto.
El momento más bajo llegó en agosto. Lombard cometió un error en seis partidos seguidos, convirtiéndose en el primer campocorto de los Yankees en hacerlo desde Roger Peckinpaugh en 1915. Acumuló siete errores en sus primeros 20 partidos de las Grandes Ligas, una cifra sorprendente para un jugador considerado un activo defensivo.
Un novato que asume la responsabilidad
Lombard no ha eludido el tema. Tras su sexto partido consecutivo con un error en agosto, abordó directamente su mala racha en lugar de restarle importancia.
Cuando le preguntaron por los errores de esa racha, Lombard se mostró sincero sobre el trabajo que le queda por delante.
«Es algo que estoy intentando averiguar», dijo Lombard.
Su entrenador le ha seguido apoyando. Aaron Boone ha calificado en varias ocasiones las dificultades de agosto como un bache pasajero y no como algo característico, y ha destacado el alcance, la potencia de lanzamiento y la capacidad atlética de Lombard como prueba de que su defensa mejorará. El novato también ha dejado entrever ese potencial con unas paradas en picado que demostraron por qué los Yankees confiaron en él de inmediato como shortstop.
El talento no está en duda. Lo que sí se cuestiona es la regularidad. Por ahora, los Yankees están dispuestos a aguantar los tropiezos iniciales porque el potencial es enorme y, al mismo tiempo que cometen errores, siguen rindiendo bien al bate.
Por qué octubre sube la apuesta
El margen de error se reduce en la postemporada, y eso es lo que convierte el desarrollo de Lombard en una de las historias más interesantes de los Yankees. Un error en agosto se diluye en una temporada de 162 partidos. Un error en un partido de playoffs puede decidir una serie.
Los Yankees apuestan por que la recompensa compense el riesgo. El bate de Lombard ha empezado a dar momentos que justifican la paciencia. Unos días antes del partido decisivo del lunes, conectó el primer grand slam de su carrera en las Grandes Ligas contra Colorado.
Ese batazo tenía su propia historia. Con 21 años y 99 días, Lombard se convirtió en el tercer jugador más joven de los Yankees en batear un grand slam, solo superado por dos jonrones de Mickey Mantle, que los bateó siendo aún más joven. Para una franquicia que se mide por sus leyendas, es un honor muy exclusivo para un novato.
«Obviamente, es intenso y cada lanzamiento cuenta, y todo importa, pero estamos preparados para ello», añadió Lombard. «La preparación va a ser la misma, la misma rutina. Solo tenemos que salir ahí fuera y hacer lo nuestro».
Ahora ha ayudado a los Yankees a llegar a otro octubre, y la recompensa por ello es una prueba aún mayor. El lunes se pudieron ver sus dos caras en tan solo unas entradas: el bate que ayudó a que Nueva York celebrara con champán y el guante que nos recordó una vez más el trabajo que aún queda por delante. Puede que su prueba más dura de este octubre no haya hecho más que empezar.
